title: Queue echo attenuation lab notes
content:
Purpose / quick TL;DR:
- Investigate a recurring small-latency amplification I see in microburst runs where queues seem to re-enqueue a small fraction of requests, creating an "echo" of work that shows as a second hump in the p95/p99 latency distribution. I call this "queue echo" and this note documents the attenuation experiments and early hypotheses.

Context / why I care:
- Customer workloads: very bursty (short spikes of ~100-400 concurrent reqs for 2–6s), mixed context lengths (avg 120 tokens, 90% < 256), and high KV cache reuse for repeated prefixes.
- We see stable p50/p90 but p95/p99 shows a shoulder ~30–80ms above baseline during bursts. Impact: higher tail SLO penalties and SLO alerts for some tenants even when aggregates look fine.

Quick hypothesis chain:
1) Some requests are being partially serviced then requeued due to transient token-generation stalls (kernel preemption / context switch / GPU warmup edge case).
2) Requeued requests hit the queue again but with slightly different priority/lane assignment -> not coalesced with their original batch -> see extra latency.
3) KV cache warm-up + slight reordering causes a small fraction (0.5–3%) to miss optimized fastpath and fall back to slow path, appearing as an echo.

Experiment design (what I ran):
- Cluster: dev-fleet-small (4x A10g), runtime build: serving-runtime@2025-01-08 + burst-attenuation-probe patch (local).
- Workload driver: loadgen v2.3, mixture: 85% short-response (40–120 toks), 15% long (300–900 toks). Zipf alpha=0.9 for client ids to mimic repeated prefixes.
- Arrival: synthetic spike generator: 0->300 qps in 250ms ramp, hold 4s, step down. 50 trials per config.
- Config knobs: coalescing window (CW) = [1ms, 4ms, 8ms, 16ms]; lane assignment: strict vs soft; preempt-delay= [0ms, 5ms]; kv-cache TTL illusions (simulated priming) on/off.

Key metrics collected:
- p50/p90/p95/p99 latency of end-to-end response (ms)
- fraction of requeue events logged by runtime (%)
- batch size distribution seen by GPU
- KV cache hit-rate by prefix (%)
- GPU utilization (%) and kernel preempt counts (where available)

Observations (raw):
- Base case (CW=4ms, soft lanes, preempt-delay=0): p95 shoulder present ~+45ms; requeue fraction ~1.8%; KV hit-rate 84%
- CW=1ms: shoulder increases to +68ms p95; requeue up to 3.2%; batch sizes slightly smaller (avg -0.6).
- CW=16ms: shoulder reduces to +18ms; requeue drops to 0.6%; batch sizes larger (avg +1.5) but tail throughput drop for long requests slightly higher (they waited longer to batch).
- preempt-delay=5ms: requeue fraction went down (~0.9%) even at CW=1ms; suggests short deferrals let kernel finish critical path.
- strict lanes: inconsistent effect — reduced requeues for hot prefixes but increased end-to-end latency variance for cold prefixes.

Simple ASCII summary (p95 delta above baseline):
- CW=1ms : +68ms (requeue 3.2%)
- CW=4ms : +45ms (requeue 1.8%)
- CW=8ms : +30ms (requeue 1.1%)
- CW=16ms: +18ms (requeue 0.6%)

Interpretation / working theory:
- The "echo" maps strongly to requeue events — when requests are re-enqueued they lose batch affinity and often miss the short-lived fastpath (KV primed BLAS kernels), which costs ~20–70ms depending on context.
- Coalescing window increases help by allowing more batching and higher chance the requeued item joins an efficient batch, but bigger CW introduces latency for single-request long tails (tradeoff).
- A small preempt-delay (5ms) acts like a micro-stall absorber: if runtime sees a micro-preemption/IO stall it defers requeue briefly and lets the in-flight kernel finish, reducing requeues.

Notes / oddities:
- In one trial CW=4ms + soft lanes we observed a correlated spike in NVidia kernel preempt counters — aligns with the preemption hypothesis, but metric granularity is poor. Need SRE to give extended kernel telemetry.
- Some requeues seem to be caused by our internal tokenizer step occasionally blocking (py GC pause spikes on host). Observe GC in host traces overlapping requeue timestamps.

Immediate mitigation ideas to test (next runs):
1) Add ephemeral preempt-delay of 3–7ms at runtime default when burst detected (adaptive). Test with production-like client mix.
2) Try hybrid coalescing: dynamic CW based on arrival variance (low-variance -> small CW; high-variance -> larger CW).
3) Ensure requeued requests carry lane affinity token so they preferentially join the same fastpath/worker for a short window.
4) Reduce host Python GC activity during bursts (GC tuning / switch hot path to minimal C-extension path).

Planned next experiments (quick plan):
- Week 1: run adaptive preempt-delay 3ms/5ms/7ms across 100 trials each, keep CW=4ms, measure p99 change and requeue fraction.
- Week 2: implement lane-affinity header prototype (soft stickiness) and measure hit-rate on KV fastpath and requeue deltas.
- Week 3: test hybrid CW algorithm under mixed multi-tenant traces (more noise).

Quick checklist / TODOs:
- [ ] Add micro GC tracing to load generator to correlate host pauses with requeues (linked to INF-2387).
- [ ] Ask SRE for kernel preempt counters at 1ms granularity for next run.
- [ ] Prototype lane-affinity propagation in worker handshake (low-risk proof-of-concept PR).
- [ ] Document results in a short deck for eng-ops weekly.

Open questions / risks:
- How will adaptive CW interact with Dedicated customers who expect strict latency SLOs? Need bounds guardrails.
- Lane-affinity could worsen fairness if a noisy tenant hoards a fastpath worker. Need eviction / TTL.

Notes-to-self (messy):
- Don't forget to check PR #4123 for race fix (might reduce 0.3% of requeues already).
- Samir said there was an old experiment where preempt-delay helped for RNN kernels — maybe reuse code.

Conclusion (draft):
- Small fraction of requests requeued explains the second hump. Short, targeted mitigations (adaptive preempt-delay + lane-affinity) look promising and low-risk to test. Bigger change (dynamic coalescing) yields better attenuation but at client-visible latency cost in some shapes.

End of notes.

-- Eden
